awd_titl_txt: Hybrid Curriculum for Upskilling Photonics Technicians in Advanced Optics and Quantum Research Enabled Technologies
awd_abstract_narration:
A significant gap exists between the state of quantum science and its practical uses in industry.  Part of the gap results from the lack of the advanced technical workforce needed to implement quantum technologies. The people best poised to enter the new quantum technological workforce are incumbent photonics technicians.  Their current qualifications provide a foundation on which to build the new quantum-related competencies. This project aims to produce a freely available curriculum that will enable photonics technicians to acquire new quantum-related competencies.  This curriculum will contain a three-course sequence with freely accessible textbooks, lab manuals, and interactive online content.  Availability of the courses via an open-access educational platform will reduce geographical barriers between colleges, students, and industry. The proposed platform can also promote the high-tech quantum workforce by increasing access to education in quantum technologies. The proposed quantum technology curriculum is expected to help U.S. businesses maintain global leadership in advanced laser and quantum technologies. 

This project will pioneer the introduction of quantum science into advanced technological education. It will do so by developing, testing, and disseminating a three-course hybrid curriculum in quantum-enabled technologies. The project will begin with an assessment of the industry demand for quantum-related skills, continue with curriculum and course development, and end with establishment of a sustainable learning platform. The three courses will be designed to meet the highest level of Quality Matters certification. The curriculum will be promoted by academic and industry collaborators and validated through data collected via the learning platform in real-time as students interact with the course material. The open-access learning platform will make the entire educational content accessible and transferrable to other institutions. Through these efforts, this project will contribute to the new quantum STEM workforce development needed to propel quantum technology forward. This project is funded by the Advanced Technological Education program that focuses on the education of technicians for the advanced-technology fields that drive the nation's economy.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The EdQuantum project, funded by the National Science Foundation under awards DUE-2055061 (Indian River State College) and DUE-2515348 (Syracuse University), set out to solve a practical problem: the United States is investing heavily in quantum technologies — in computing, communication, sensing, and advanced manufacturing — but there are not enough trained workers to support this growing industry. EdQuantum was designed to close this gap by developing a complete, accessible educational program that prepares students and working professionals for careers in quantum and photonics technologies.

Over five years, the project produced a full three-course curriculum covering the fundamentals of quantum optics, quantum hardware and software, and spectroscopy — the science of using light to identify and analyze materials. All three courses are now publicly available on Udemy, an online learning platform, reaching learners in multiple countries across the globe. Each course includes a textbook, laboratory experiment guides, recorded demonstration videos, quizzes, and other learning resources. All three textbooks are being published by SPIE, the leading international society in optics and photonics, making them permanently available to educators and learners worldwide.

One of the project's most important achievements is the breadth of people it has reached. EdQuantum was originally designed for community college students and photonics technicians. It has served that audience well, with successful pilots at SUNY Broome Community College and SUNY Jefferson Community College in Central New York and Indian River State College in Florida. But the curriculum has proven effective far beyond that original audience. High school students explored quantum science through a summer program at Syracuse University and through a quantum club at Jamesville-DeWitt High School. University freshmen engaged with the material through an informal quantum club at Syracuse University. Adult career changers and veterans used EdQuantum materials through a separate workforce development program designed to help people enter the semiconductor and quantum industries in Central New York. Industry professionals — including sales engineers, product managers, and business leaders — attended workshops at the SPIE Photonics West conference, one of the largest optics and photonics events in the world, where EdQuantum-based courses attracted nearly 30 participants in a single session. Online learners from seven countries enrolled within the first weeks of the Udemy launch. This range of audiences — from high school through professional practice, from upstate New York to international learners — demonstrates that quantum education does not have to be limited to research universities or students with advanced science backgrounds.

The project unfolded in two distinct phases. The first phase, based at Indian River State College in Florida, gave the team direct access to a community college environment where the curriculum was developed and first tested with students. The second phase, based at Syracuse University in New York, brought the project into a research university setting with stronger grant infrastructure and closer proximity to the quantum and semiconductor industries of Central New York, enabling broader dissemination and deeper community partnerships.

A significant hands-on component of the project is the portable quantum laboratory kit, developed in the final year of the project. This compact, self-contained kit uses simple optical components to demonstrate fundamental quantum principles and can be transported in a suitcase and set up anywhere — a classroom, a conference room, or a community center. Eight identical kits were built and deployed at national conferences and partner institutions. Students at SUNY Broome Community College who worked with this kit won the Community College Innovation Challenge, a nationally competitive NSF-supported program that recognizes community college students applying science to real-world problems. This outcome is a powerful reminder that students at two-year colleges, given the right tools and encouragement, can compete and innovate at the national level.

The EdQuantum project has shown that quantum education can be made accessible, portable, and relevant to a wide range of people. As quantum technologies continue to reshape industries and create new careers, the curriculum, textbooks, videos, and laboratory tools developed through this project will remain freely available to educators, students, and institutions across the country and around the world.
